skills.when_to_use: Use for any multi-video question requiring visual evidence combined across videos, where the Global Planner must coordinate evidence collection and submit the final answer. Applicable from the start of the question, before any evidence is collected, since selection input is only the question, video IDs and durations; it covers the whole decision process including branching, refinement and the final answer, with no other card activated.
skills.strategy: Goal: submit parameters.answer for the complete question using visual evidence from at least two videos. Prerequisite: you are the text-only Global Planner; private VideoAgent observations are invisible to you, so rely only on public History and facts explicitly returned to you. Do not answer from metadata (IDs, durations, option wording) alone. Procedure: 1) From the question, list the distinct visual facts or relationships needed and which videos plausibly hold them. Separate (a) per-video facts, each observable inside one video, from (b) cross-video visual relationships (same action/object correspondence, relative motion, style or appearance differences, temporal alignment across videos). 2) Check History first: any fact already returned by a prior analyze_videos or watch_videos result is reusable; do not re-request it. 3) For per-video facts, use analyze_videos with one self-contained instruction per video: copy the video_id exactly, make each instruction independently understandable (the agent sees only its video and that instruction), and ask only for what is visually observable in that video, not computed answers or cross-video mappings. Batch several videos in one action when their facts are independent; keep total instruction text within the 3600-character shared limit and floor(3600/N) per instruction. 4) For cross-video visual relationships, use watch_videos: select 2-4 distinct listed videos, one clip each with complete start/end seconds inside each video's duration; the instruction string is the entire prompt to the visual model, so name the videos by ID, state the exact visible relationship to compare, and request concise natural-language analysis, never the final answer. Prefer short clips when the target detail is brief or fine-grained; longer total duration gives broader coverage but sparser sampling. Do not include fps. 5) Branching: if returned facts are vague, contradictory, or a needed element (e.g., a specific time, object, or attribute) is missing, issue a follow-up action: either a new analyze_videos instruction that embeds the previously returned facts as context for the relevant video, or a targeted watch_videos on narrowed clips. Continue such checks only while a permitted observation could change the judgment; with at most 5 ordinary decision steps, plan to batch evidence requests rather than one per fact. 6) Combine: cross-video facts come from watch_videos results or from juxtaposing per-video facts you yourself compare in text. When History sufficiently supports a judgment, or further checks cannot help, choose answer: give a concise evidence-based reason citing which videos and observations support it, note any material uncertainty, and put the requested answer representation in parameters.answer (if options are given, use only the selected option label or explicitly requested text). Never submit an unsupported guess when a permitted observation could still discriminate among candidates; but once evidence is sufficient or exhausted, submit the best-supported judgment rather than a discussion of missing evidence.
